cards.prompt: In the Python Agent SDK, you set a tool denylist on a ClaudeAgentOptions object and on an AgentDefinition object. Which casing does each take?
cards.answer: ClaudeAgentOptions takes snake_case (disallowed_tools); AgentDefinition takes camelCase (disallowedTools)

choices: Both take snake_case, because the whole package is Python and Python is snake_case
ClaudeAgentOptions takes snake_case (disallowed_tools); AgentDefinition takes camelCase (disallowedTools)
ClaudeAgentOptions takes camelCase (disallowedTools); AgentDefinition takes snake_case (disallowed_tools)
Both take camelCase, because both mirror the Claude Code JSON settings surface
metadata.explanation: The same concept takes both spellings inside one import. ClaudeAgentOptions is the Python-shaped options object you construct (snake_case); AgentDefinition mirrors subagent markdown frontmatter, which is Claude Code-shaped (camelCase). The casing is a property of the OBJECT, not of the concept — so the word alone can never answer it.

cards.prompt: Which four ClaudeAgentOptions fields have same-named camelCase twins on AgentDefinition?
cards.answer: disallowed_tools, mcp_servers, max_turns, permission_mode

choices: allowed_tools, system_prompt, model, cwd
hooks, agents, setting_sources, settings
disallowed_tools, mcp_servers, max_turns, permission_mode
resume, fork_session, add_dirs, env
metadata.explanation: The verified pairs are disallowed_tools/disallowedTools, mcp_servers/mcpServers, max_turns/maxTurns, permission_mode/permissionMode. AgentDefinition's full field set is description, prompt, tools, model, disallowedTools, mcpServers, maxTurns, permissionMode.

cards.prompt: To run Claude Code's agent loop from inside your own Python service, what do you import — and what is NOT importable?
cards.answer: Import claude_agent_sdk; claude_code is the CLI binary, not a package — importing it raises ImportError

choices: Import claude_code; claude_agent_sdk is the TypeScript-only distribution
Import claude_agent_sdk; claude_code is the CLI binary, not a package — importing it raises ImportError
Import anthropic.claude_code; the Agent SDK is only a thin wrapper over it
Either works — claude_code is an alias that re-exports claude_agent_sdk
metadata.explanation: CLI you run, SDK you import. The pip package is claude-agent-sdk (TypeScript twin: @anthropic-ai/claude-agent-sdk). claude-code is a program, not a library.

cards.prompt: In the Agent SDK, what is the difference between query() and ClaudeSDKClient?
cards.answer: query() is one-shot — a new session per call, returning an async iterator of messages; ClaudeSDKClient holds a persistent session across exchanges

choices: query() is one-shot — a new session per call, returning an async iterator of messages; ClaudeSDKClient holds a persistent session across exchanges
query() is synchronous and blocking; ClaudeSDKClient is the async version of the same one-shot call
query() runs locally against the CLI; ClaudeSDKClient calls the hosted Anthropic agent service
query() is the streaming interface; ClaudeSDKClient is the batch interface for many prompts at once
metadata.explanation: query() = new session per call, returns an async iterator. ClaudeSDKClient = persistent session, with connect(), receive_response() and interrupt().

cards.prompt: Which SDK message type is the terminal one, on which stop_reason surfaces?
cards.answer: ResultMessage

choices: AssistantMessage
ResultMessage
SystemMessage
FinalMessage
metadata.explanation: ResultMessage is the terminal message type. Note that stop_reason is an API (BODY-bin) word riding up through the SDK — its home is the Messages API, not the SDK.

cards.prompt: Your loop branches on `if stop_reason == "tool_use": continue else: done`. Which two stop_reason values make that wrong?
cards.answer: max_tokens and refusal — both produce tool-call-free text that looks finished but isn't

choices: end_turn and stop_sequence — both can be emitted mid-tool-call
pause_turn and end_turn — both mean the server wants the response passed back
stop_sequence and pause_turn — both are silent truncations
max_tokens and refusal — both produce tool-call-free text that looks finished but isn't
metadata.explanation: Branch on stop_reason, never on whether text contains a tool call. end_turn = done. max_tokens = truncated, not done. refusal = declined for safety, possibly with no text block at all. Lumping those into the else-branch is exactly the bug.

cards.prompt: Name all six stop_reason values the Messages API can return in an agentic loop.
cards.answer: tool_use, end_turn, max_tokens, stop_sequence, pause_turn, refusal

choices: tool_use, end_turn, max_tokens, stop_sequence, pause_turn, refusal
tool_use, end_turn, max_tokens, stop_sequence, error, timeout
tool_use, end_turn, max_tokens, content_filter, length, refusal
tool_call, complete, truncated, stop_sequence, paused, refused
metadata.explanation: pause_turn means a long server-tool turn paused — pass the response straight back. max_tokens means truncated, not done.

cards.prompt: In the tool loop, what must you append to `messages` before appending the tool_result — and what happens if you skip it?
cards.answer: Append the assistant turn containing the tool_use block first; skip it and the tool_result has no matching tool_use, giving a 400

choices: Append the assistant turn containing the tool_use block first; skip it and the tool_result has no matching tool_use, giving a 400
Append a system turn restating the tool contract first; skip it and the model re-calls the same tool forever
Append an empty user turn as a separator first; skip it and the roles alternate incorrectly, giving a 429
Nothing — the tool_result may be appended directly, and the API reconstructs the pairing from tool_use_id
metadata.explanation: The tool_use_id in your tool_result must resolve to a tool_use block that is already in the conversation. Appending the assistant turn first is the loop-wiring rule.

cards.prompt: Subagent #3 is blocked and needs something subagent #1 produced. What is the correct channel?
cards.answer: It returns structured control up to the coordinator, which decides what happens next

choices: It messages subagent #1 directly over the peer channel the coordinator opened for them
It writes to the shared scratchpad that all subagents poll between steps
It returns structured control up to the coordinator, which decides what happens next
It re-spawns subagent #1 as its own child so the dependency stays local
metadata.explanation: Hub-and-spoke: subagents never talk peer-to-peer. The three reasons are auditability, loop-safety and context isolation. What travels up is structured control, not prose.

cards.prompt: Four parallel subagents write DB rows; #3 fails on a rate limit. Why is 're-run all four' wrong?
cards.answer: The other three already wrote rows, so a blanket re-run duplicates side effects — retry only the failed unit

choices: The other three would exceed the same rate limit, so re-running all four guarantees four failures
The other three already wrote rows, so a blanket re-run duplicates side effects — retry only the failed unit
Re-running all four resets the coordinator's context window and loses the original plan
Nothing is wrong with it — blanket retry is the standard recovery pattern for parallel fan-out
metadata.explanation: This is correctness, not just cost. A rate limit is transient, so #3 should back off and retry locally first; escalate to the coordinator only if it genuinely cannot. Ties to D5 idempotency.

cards.prompt: Which of these is NOT a valid ground for spawning a subagent?
cards.answer: The task is multi-step

choices: The task needs context isolation from the parent
The task needs a different permission boundary
The task can run concurrently with other work
The task is multi-step
metadata.explanation: The three grounds are context isolation, permission boundary, and concurrency. 'It has several steps' is not one — a multi-step task is just a loop.

cards.prompt: A coordinator answers 'how does user-export work?' covering only REST controllers; scheduled jobs, admin actions and CLI paths are missing. Every subagent completed successfully. Root cause?
cards.answer: The coordinator's decomposition — it never enumerated the other entry points, so this is a missing assignment, not a missing capability

choices: The coordinator's decomposition — it never enumerated the other entry points, so this is a missing assignment, not a missing capability
The subagents' tool grants — none of them could read the job scheduler or CLI source, so their coverage was capped
The coordinator's context window — the earlier subagent results crowded out the later entry points before synthesis
The subagent prompts — each was too narrow, so the fix is to widen each prompt to 'inspect everything related to export'
metadata.explanation: The discriminator is 'did anyone fail?' Every worker succeeded, so nothing a worker needed was missing. Spawning more subagents to cover the other paths requires YOU to already know the paths — it fixes the instance, not the system. Scope note: if a worker HAD failed or returned partial, capability could genuinely be the fault.

cards.prompt: Both parallelization and orchestrator-workers fan out to workers. What is the one tell that separates them?
cards.answer: Whether the subtasks are pre-known (parallelization) or discovered per-input at runtime (orchestrator-workers)

choices: Whether the workers run concurrently (parallelization) or sequentially (orchestrator-workers)
Whether the subtasks are pre-known (parallelization) or discovered per-input at runtime (orchestrator-workers)
Whether the workers share a context window (parallelization) or each get an isolated one (orchestrator-workers)
Whether there is a final aggregation step (parallelization) or the workers write directly (orchestrator-workers)
metadata.explanation: Parallelism and isolated context are shared by both, so neither is the tell. 'Translate into these five fixed languages' = parallelization. 'Refactor across an unpredictable set of files' = orchestrator-workers.

cards.prompt: Which axis separates prompt chaining from orchestrator-workers?
cards.answer: Sequential vs adaptive decomposition — whether the plan is fixed in code or discovered at runtime

choices: Single-model vs multi-model — chaining reuses one model, orchestrators dispatch across tiers
Stateless vs stateful — chaining passes state forward, orchestrators hold it centrally
Cost vs latency — chaining optimises tokens, orchestrators optimise wall-clock
Sequential vs adaptive decomposition — whether the plan is fixed in code or discovered at runtime
metadata.explanation: Both decompose. Chaining's decomposition is written by you in advance; the orchestrator's is produced by a model at runtime.

cards.prompt: (a) The agent must verify the customer before it may refund. (b) The agent escalates easy cases and attempts hard ones. Which is fixed with code and which with a prompt?
cards.answer: (a) code — a checkable precondition gating the refund tool; (b) prompt — explicit escalation criteria plus examples

choices: (a) prompt — state the verification requirement clearly; (b) code — a confidence threshold that routes to a human
Both code — protection is always code the model cannot talk its way around
(a) code — a checkable precondition gating the refund tool; (b) prompt — explicit escalation criteria plus examples
Both prompt — both are policy decisions, and policy belongs in the system prompt
metadata.explanation: The discriminator is: is the condition CHECKABLE? A required sequence with a boolean can be gated. 'Is this case complex enough?' is a judgment with no boolean — you can only specify it. 'Protection is code you write' has an edge, and this is it.

cards.prompt: Four failures. Which one's correct fix lives at the STRUCTURE layer rather than the INSTRUCTION layer? (i) invoice JSON arrives wrapped in markdown fences a few percent of the time (ii) a 600-line CLAUDE.md is increasingly ignored (iii) guidance is needed for every *.test.tsx wherever it lives
cards.answer: (i) only — a downstream parser needs a guarantee, so the shape must come from a tool schema, not from wording

choices: (ii) only — file bloat is a structural defect and must be solved with @import splitting
(iii) only — path-scoped guidance requires a hook that matches on the file path
All three — a guarantee is always preferable to an instruction when both are available
(i) only — a downstream parser needs a guarantee, so the shape must come from a tool schema, not from wording
metadata.explanation: The decider: does something downstream need a GUARANTEE? A guarantee cannot be probabilistic, so it has to live in the mechanism. A preference or a piece of guidance needs no guarantee, and there the instruction layer is the correct and cheaper tool, not a weak substitute. 'Always pick the structural option' is the next failure.

cards.prompt: A document-analysis subagent has a generic fetch_url tool and keeps citing blogs it found linked inside the approved PDFs. Best fix?
cards.answer: Replace fetch_url with a validating load_document tool that only resolves approved sources

choices: Add a CLAUDE.md rule stating that only the approved PDFs may be cited
Replace fetch_url with a validating load_document tool that only resolves approved sources
Add few-shot examples of good citations to the subagent's prompt
Lower the subagent's temperature so it stops following speculative links
metadata.explanation: A permission boundary needs a guarantee, and a guarantee cannot be probabilistic. The tool contract is the mechanism that produced the failure and you own it — so change it rather than asking the model more firmly.

cards.prompt: The exam offers 'switch to a higher-tier model' as an option. When is it the keyed answer?
cards.answer: Almost never — but genuinely when the stem says the criteria are already precise and correctly applied elsewhere

choices: Whenever the agent's failures are inconsistent between runs, since inconsistency is a capability signal
Whenever the task involves multi-step reasoning, since smaller models cannot chain reliably
Almost never — but genuinely when the stem says the criteria are already precise and correctly applied elsewhere
Never — a model upgrade is always a distractor on this exam, without exception
metadata.explanation: If the stem names a fixable design defect (vague criteria, a starved tool description, a missing gate), the model-upgrade option is the distractor: a definitionally-broken prompt does not become correct on a bigger model. The other half is real but rare — a sound prompt a small model simply cannot apply is a capability failure.

cards.prompt: An agent has a hard safety limit ('never refund more than $500'). Where does it belong?
cards.answer: In code the model cannot talk its way around, because the condition is checkable

choices: In the system prompt, stated as an absolute rule with emphasis
In code the model cannot talk its way around, because the condition is checkable
In the tool's description, so the model sees it at selection time
In a few-shot example showing a refusal at $501
metadata.explanation: This is the checkable half of the rule. A dollar threshold is a boolean; gate it. Contrast the judgment half — 'when should this escalate?' — which can only be specified in the prompt.

cards.prompt: A subagent needs one capability for 85% of its cases; the remaining 15% need the coordinator's full toolset. What do you grant?
cards.answer: A single scoped tool for the 85% case, leaving the coordinator delegation intact for the 15%

choices: A single scoped tool for the 85% case, leaving the coordinator delegation intact for the 15%
The full toolset, since the subagent will eventually need all of it anyway
Nothing new — batch the needs and hand them all to the coordinator at the end of the run
A speculative pre-cache of likely results, so the subagent rarely has to call out at all
metadata.explanation: Least privilege: right-size the grant to the common case. Handing over the full toolset fixes latency and destroys separation of concerns plus the coordinator's audit trail. Batching to the end creates blocking dependencies when later steps depend on earlier verified facts.

cards.prompt: A field named inputSchema and a field named input_schema both exist. Which surface owns which?
cards.answer: inputSchema is the MCP wire (camelCase); input_schema is the Messages API request body (snake_case)

choices: inputSchema is the Messages API request body; input_schema is the MCP wire
inputSchema is the TypeScript SDK; input_schema is the Python SDK — same surface, two languages
They are aliases on the same surface and the API accepts either spelling
inputSchema is the MCP wire (camelCase); input_schema is the Messages API request body (snake_case)
metadata.explanation: The Messages API body is snake_case; the MCP protocol is camelCase. Same concept, two surfaces, two spellings — and every such pair is a distractor the exam can build a question out of.

cards.prompt: Match the four MCP↔API casing pairs: the tool failed, why generation stopped, the content type label, the list changed.
cards.answer: is_error/isError, stop_reason:"end_turn"/stopReason:"endTurn", mimeType (MCP only), listChanged (MCP only)

choices: is_error/isError, stop_reason:"end_turn"/stopReason:"endTurn", mimeType (MCP only), listChanged (MCP only)
isError/is_error, stopReason/stop_reason, mime_type (API only), list_changed (API only)
error/isError, reason/stopReason, contentType/mimeType, changed/listChanged
is_error and isError are different concepts; the rest have no cross-surface twin
metadata.explanation: MCP re-implements half the Messages API's vocabulary in camelCase. mimeType and listChanged have no Messages API twin at all — they are MCP-only.

cards.prompt: Casing alone won't settle it. What is the test that always works?
cards.answer: Ask who is talking to whom: a field in the JSON you POST to api.anthropic.com is BODY; a field in a JSON-RPC message between a client and a separate server process is PROCESS

choices: Ask which SDK exposes it: if it appears in the Python SDK it is BODY, otherwise it is PROCESS
Ask whether Anthropic documents it: Anthropic-documented fields are BODY, community-documented fields are PROCESS
Ask who is talking to whom: a field in the JSON you POST to api.anthropic.com is BODY; a field in a JSON-RPC message between a client and a separate server process is PROCESS
Ask how long the identifier is: BODY fields are short and single-word, PROCESS fields are namespaced
metadata.explanation: tool_choice is something you tell the model, so BODY. roots is something a client tells a server, so PROCESS. Casing is a fast check, never a proof — it breaks entirely on your own JSON payloads, where the casing is whatever you chose.

cards.prompt: Bin each: is_path_allowed · tool_choice · acceptEdits · is_error · roots · allowed_tools · stateless_http
cards.answer: MCP · API · Claude Code · API · MCP · Claude Code · MCP

choices: API · MCP · Claude Code · MCP · API · Agent SDK · Claude Code
MCP · API · Claude Code · API · MCP · Claude Code · MCP
MCP · API · Agent SDK · API · MCP · Agent SDK · Claude Code
Agent SDK · API · Claude Code · API · Agent SDK · Claude Code · MCP
metadata.explanation: The most-missed item in the whole deck. The word never decides the bin — where you EXPRESS it does. stateless_http SOUNDS like infrastructure config, so it feels like Claude Code; it is a FastMCP server flag. A term that NAMES a surface is the signal to check the other axis.

cards.prompt: Bin each: tool_use · tools/call · /mcp__github__review · resources/read · .mcp.json · initialize
cards.answer: Messages API · MCP · Claude Code · MCP · Claude Code · MCP

choices: MCP · MCP · MCP · MCP · Claude Code · MCP
Messages API · Messages API · Claude Code · MCP · Claude Code · Messages API
Messages API · MCP · Claude Code · MCP · Claude Code · MCP
Messages API · MCP · MCP · MCP · MCP · MCP
metadata.explanation: The tell ladder: tool_use / input_schema → API. A slash-separated JSON-RPC method (x/y) → MCP. An mcp__ prefix, an @, a slash-command or a dotfile → the client's own surface.

cards.prompt: Does the Messages API contain any MCP?
cards.answer: No — none whatsoever; MCP is one optional way a client may fulfil a tool_use block

choices: No — none whatsoever; MCP is one optional way a client may fulfil a tool_use block
Yes — tools/call is the Messages API's internal name for a tool invocation
Yes — the Messages API embeds the MCP handshake whenever tools are present
Only for server tools like web_search, which are implemented as built-in MCP servers
metadata.explanation: Three stacked layers, and the exam tests the seams. MCP is an open spec that non-Anthropic apps speak; 'MCP is how Claude calls tools' is false. Plenty of tool use involves no MCP at all.

cards.prompt: In a multi-turn tool loop, how often must the `tools` array be sent?
cards.answer: On every request in the loop, not just the first

choices: Only on the first request; the API caches the definitions for the session
Only when the definitions change from the previous turn
On every request in the loop, not just the first
Once per tool_use_id; re-sending them invalidates the pairing
metadata.explanation: The Messages API is stateless. Every call carries the full tools array, which is also why adding a tool invalidates a cache prefix — tools sit at the front.

cards.prompt: Which field on a tool definition is the model's selection mechanism?
cards.answer: description — the model picks by description, not by name

choices: name — the model matches the user's phrasing against the tool name
input_schema — the model picks whichever schema its intended arguments satisfy
description — the model picks by description, not by name
the array position — earlier tools are tried first
metadata.explanation: This is why two tools with thin descriptions ('Retrieves customer information' / 'Retrieves order details') is a schema defect, not a prompt problem. The description is the API the model programs against.

cards.prompt: What does `strict: true` on a custom tool definition buy you?
cards.answer: Constrained decoding — the call is guaranteed to conform exactly to the input_schema

choices: A validation pass after generation, with an automatic retry when the arguments fail
A guarantee that the model will call the tool rather than answering in text
Constrained decoding — the call is guaranteed to conform exactly to the input_schema
A guarantee that the argument VALUES are semantically correct, not just well-typed
metadata.explanation: strict:true restricts the sampler to a grammar derived from your schema, so invalid JSON is impossible by construction. It still guarantees only SHAPE — a schema saying total:number is satisfied by a wrong total.

cards.prompt: Name the four tool_choice values, and say which one guarantees a call while letting the model pick which tool.
cards.answer: auto, any, tool, none — and `any` guarantees a call while letting the model pick

choices: auto, any, tool, none — and `any` guarantees a call while letting the model pick
auto, required, named, off — and `required` guarantees a call while letting the model pick
auto, any, tool, none — and `tool` guarantees a call while letting the model pick
default, acceptEdits, plan, bypassPermissions — and `plan` guarantees a call
metadata.explanation: auto = may tool or text (default). any = must call SOME tool, model picks. {type:tool,name} = must call THAT tool. none = may not call. Note the fourth option is Claude Code's permission modes — a different quartet of four mode names, and a documented interference trap.

cards.prompt: When tool_choice forces a call (any or a named tool), what stop_reason comes back?
cards.answer: Always tool_use — never end_turn

choices: Always tool_use — never end_turn
Always end_turn, because the forced call terminates the turn
stop_sequence, because forcing inserts an implicit stop sequence
It varies: any gives tool_use, a named tool gives end_turn
metadata.explanation: Forcing means the turn cannot end without a tool call, so the stop_reason is always tool_use. The named form is the forced-extraction / structured-output trick.

cards.prompt: You want at most one tool call per turn. Which key, and where does it go?
cards.answer: disable_parallel_tool_use — a key INSIDE the tool_choice object

choices: disable_parallel_tool_use — a top-level request parameter beside tool_choice
disable_parallel_tool_use — a key INSIDE the tool_choice object
max_parallel_tools: 1 — a top-level request parameter
parallel_tool_calls: false — a key inside each tool definition
metadata.explanation: It is a sibling of `type` inside tool_choice, not a parameter beside it.

cards.prompt: Which field links a tool_result back to the model's call, and how do you flag a tool failure?
cards.answer: tool_use_id must equal the tool_use block's id; flag failure with is_error: true and still send the result

choices: tool_call_id must equal the tool_use block's name; flag failure by omitting the result entirely
tool_use_id must equal the tool_use block's id; flag failure by raising an exception in your handler
tool_result_id is generated by you; flag failure with a non-zero exit code from the handler
tool_use_id must equal the tool_use block's id; flag failure with is_error: true and still send the result
metadata.explanation: Omitting a failed result breaks the pairing and gives a 400. Errors are data you send back, not exceptions you throw.

cards.prompt: Which role does a tool_result block live in?
cards.answer: A user turn — the tool does not get a role of its own

choices: A user turn — the tool does not get a role of its own
A tool turn — the API defines a third role for exactly this
An assistant turn — it continues the assistant's tool_use turn
A system turn — results are injected as authoritative context
metadata.explanation: There are only user and assistant roles (plus the top-level `system` parameter, which is a parameter, not a message). Tool results ride in a user turn.

cards.prompt: What form does the `content` of a tool_result take?
cards.answer: A string — json.dumps your dict before sending it

choices: A string — json.dumps your dict before sending it
A native JSON object, which the API validates against the tool's input_schema
A list of content blocks, one per return field
A base64-encoded payload, so binary results are supported uniformly
metadata.explanation: It is a string. Serialize structured results yourself.

cards.prompt: A teammate says 'the text editor tool is Anthropic-defined, so we just read the result out of the response — no handler needed.' Correct them.
cards.answer: Wrong — text_editor is an Anthropic-schema CLIENT tool: Anthropic publishes the schema, but YOUR app executes it and returns the tool_result

choices: Wrong — text_editor is an Anthropic-schema CLIENT tool: Anthropic publishes the schema, but YOUR app executes it and returns the tool_result
Right — Anthropic-defined tools are executed by Anthropic and the result arrives in the same response
Wrong — text_editor is a server tool, so it needs no handler but does need an explicit beta header
Right for text_editor specifically, but wrong for bash and computer, which you must execute
metadata.explanation: 'Anthropic-defined' is not 'Anthropic-executed'. Three families: your own tools (you write the schema, you execute); Anthropic-schema client tools — memory, bash, text_editor, computer (you pass only {type, name} with NO input_schema, and you still execute); server tools (Anthropic runs them, result already in the response, no tool_result loop).

cards.prompt: Sort by who executes: text_editor · web_search · computer · code_execution
cards.answer: You · Anthropic · You · Anthropic

choices: You · Anthropic · You · Anthropic
You · Anthropic · You · You
Anthropic · Anthropic · You · Anthropic
You · You · You · Anthropic
metadata.explanation: The seam word is WHERE THE CODE RUNS, never who wrote the schema. code_execution is a SERVER tool — Anthropic runs the sandbox, you enable it and get results back. The counter-case that stops the rule over-firing: web_search is Anthropic-defined AND Anthropic-executed, so 'it's Anthropic-defined' is evidence for neither side.

cards.prompt: Which of these are server tools — run at Anthropic, with results already in the response and no tool_result loop?
cards.answer: web_search, web_fetch, code_execution (plus tool_search and advisor)

choices: web_search, web_fetch, code_execution (plus tool_search and advisor)
bash, text_editor, memory, computer
web_search, bash, memory, computer
Only web_search; everything else requires a handler you write
metadata.explanation: Server tools need no handler code at all. Client tools — even Anthropic-schema ones — always come back to you.

cards.prompt: Two sibling tools have thin descriptions and similar inputs; the model keeps picking the wrong one. Most effective FIRST step?
cards.answer: Expand both descriptions with input formats, example queries, edge cases and explicit boundaries against the sibling

choices: Expand both descriptions with input formats, example queries, edge cases and explicit boundaries against the sibling
Add few-shot examples to the system prompt showing which tool to use when
Add a routing layer that classifies the request before the model sees the tools
Consolidate them into one lookup_entity tool with an action parameter
metadata.explanation: Descriptions ARE the selection mechanism, so thin descriptions are the root cause, not a symptom. Few-shot pays tokens every turn to compensate for a starved description and only covers the shapes you thought to write. A routing layer is over-engineered; consolidation is a legitimate architecture change but far too heavy for a first step.

cards.prompt: A tool description says 'never call this without user confirmation.' It fires anyway. What can a description enforce?
cards.answer: Nothing — a description is input to a probabilistic decision function; it shifts likelihood and cannot constrain

choices: It enforces the constraint whenever the model is above a certain capability tier
Nothing — a description is input to a probabilistic decision function; it shifts likelihood and cannot constrain
It enforces the constraint only if the same sentence also appears in the system prompt
It enforces the constraint at the API layer, which rejects calls that violate stated preconditions
metadata.explanation: Same class as MCP roots: advisory. Rewording it 'more explicitly' is the wrong fix CLASS. What stops the call is code in the CLIENT that gates before it executes the function. Descriptions persuade; code prevents.

cards.prompt: Why split a calendar tool into create/update/cancel rather than one manage_calendar(action, ...)?
cards.answer: Distinct required fields per action — one combined tool forces every field optional, so incomplete creates get through; and cancel is destructive, so it deserves its own permission

choices: Efficiency — three small schemas are cheaper to send than one large one
Discoverability — the model reads tool names before descriptions, so three names are easier to match
Rate limiting — separate tools can be throttled independently
Distinct required fields per action — one combined tool forces every field optional, so incomplete creates get through; and cancel is destructive, so it deserves its own permission
metadata.explanation: The mechanism is the schema, not efficiency. A combined tool cannot express 'attendees are required for create but meaningless for cancel', so it degrades to all-optional and loses the contract.

cards.prompt: What shape should a tool error take when you return it to the model?
cards.answer: An actionable message the MODEL can act on — 'this event is in the past; use update_event instead of cancelling'

choices: The upstream status code and body verbatim, so nothing is lost in translation
An actionable message the MODEL can act on — 'this event is in the past; use update_event instead of cancelling'
A short opaque code the client maps to a message, keeping tokens low
An exception, so the loop terminates and the caller can decide
metadata.explanation: Errors are for the model, not the engineer. 'Error 422' tells it nothing it can do differently. Note that errorCategory/isRetryable are YOUR payload — the MCP-vs-API casing rule does not apply to your own JSON.

cards.prompt: Match each MCP primitive to who controls it: tools, resources, prompts.
cards.answer: tools = model-controlled · resources = application-driven · prompts = user-controlled

choices: tools = model-controlled · resources = model-controlled · prompts = application-driven
tools = application-driven · resources = user-controlled · prompts = model-controlled
tools = model-controlled · resources = application-driven · prompts = user-controlled
All three are model-controlled; the categories describe who registers them, not who invokes them

cards.prompt: Accuracy degrades deep in a long session, BEFORE the window is full. Cause, fix, and what does NOT fix it?

cards.prompt: Progressive summarization under a hard budget, support case. Which survives — the order number, or whether the refund happened?

metadata.explanation: This inverts the intuition, which is why it is carded. In a support case the identifiers ARE the payload, so a summarizer keeps the numbers and sheds the pleasantries — measured 4/4 even squeezed to 90 tokens. Meanwhile 'customer requesting refund; return received' compresses one notch into 'refund processed' and nothing looks wrong. Compaction eats your tense, not your numbers. Note which failure is worse: a lost identifier makes the agent ASK; drifted state makes it DECLINE TO ACT while every number in the reply is correct.

cards.prompt: A multi-agent run crashes. You scan the output directory, every output you find is complete, and you report success. What did you miss?

choices: A worker whose output was written but corrupted mid-flush, which a completeness check would catch

metadata.explanation: A listing answers 'what happened?'; recovery asks 'what was supposed to happen?' and no amount of reading the output can answer it. THE ONE LINE: record_dispatch() is called BEFORE the worker runs, so the manifest records an INTENTION, not a completion. Move it after the work and the manifest degrades into a directory listing with extra steps. Keep `attempted` and `completed` as SEPARATE fields or you cannot tell never-started from started-and-died.

cards.prompt: The manifest says a worker was DISPATCHED but produced NO OUTPUT. Is re-running it safe?

metadata.explanation: NO CHECKPOINT DOES NOT MEAN NO EFFECT. 'No output' is evidence about your disk, not about a payment processor. Repeatable (re-encode a file, overwrite a row) → state is a speed optimisation, re-run. Non-repeatable (charge, email, ship, webhook) → the checkpoint is the only thing between you and doing it twice. 'Wipe and start clean' sounds conservative and DOUBLE-BILLS. And reordering checkpoint-and-charge does not fix it — every order has a window; the fix is an IDEMPOTENCY KEY the processor deduplicates on.
